sessions.title: Day 1 · Sit and breathe
script: Hello, and welcome to your very first day.
If you've never meditated before, you're in exactly the right place.
For the next five minutes, there's nothing to get right. No score, no right or wrong way to do this.
Your only job is to be here. And you already are.
Before we start, let's clear up a very common misunderstanding.
A lot of people think meditating means emptying your mind. Not thinking about anything at all.
If that were true, almost nobody could do it.
Meditation is really about noticing. Noticing what's happening inside you and around you, while it's happening.
Thoughts will keep coming. That's normal. It's simply what your brain does all day long.
You're just going to learn to watch them pass, and to come back to something very simple: your breath.
Let's start by getting settled.
Sit on a chair, on your sofa, or on a cushion, wherever feels comfortable.
If you're on a chair, place both feet flat on the floor, roughly hip-width apart.
Let your back lengthen, as if a thread were gently drawing the top of your head toward the ceiling.
Upright, but not stiff. You're not standing to attention. You're just here, steady and at ease.
Let your shoulders drop a little, away from your ears.
Rest your hands on your thighs or your knees, palms up or palms down, whichever you prefer.
Now, you can close your eyes.
If you'd rather keep them open, that's absolutely fine. Just let your gaze rest on the floor, about a meter in front of you, without focusing on anything.
[pause 3s]
To really arrive here, we'll take three breaths that are a little deeper than usual.
Nothing forced. Just a bit more air, and a bit more slowness.
Breathe in through your nose, unhurried, letting your belly rise.
And breathe out through your mouth, slowly, like a long sigh.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in, feeling your chest open a little.
And breathe out, letting your shoulders soften as the air leaves.
[pause 3s]
One last time. Breathe in gently.
And let it all go as you breathe out.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breathing find its own natural rhythm. You don't need to steer it anymore. It's always known how to breathe on its own.
Your job is simply to watch it.
Look for the place where you feel your breath most clearly.
Maybe at the edge of your nostrils, where the air feels a little cooler coming in, and a little warmer going out.
Maybe in your chest, rising and falling.
Or maybe in your belly, gently swelling as you breathe in, and softening as you breathe out.
There's no right place. Just choose wherever it feels clearest for you, today.
And stay there, with that one spot.
Feel the very beginning of the in-breath, the moment the air arrives.
Then the tiny moment at the top, where everything pauses.
And the out-breath, flowing away, with no effort at all.
For the next minute, I'll speak softly, and not very much. You'll simply follow your breath, one breath after another.
If a thought shows up, and it will, that's not a problem. You notice it, and you come back to the breath.
That's it. That really is all there is to it.
One breath in. One breath out. You don't need to count them, or make them perfect.
You might notice they don't last the same amount of time. Often, the air takes a little longer to leave than it does to arrive.
If your mind has wandered off, you've just noticed it. That's exactly what meditating is. Come back, without judging yourself.
Just this breath. Not the last one, not the next one.
If your body needs to move a little, go ahead, slowly, and then find your breath again.
A few more breaths, at your own pace. The air coming in. The air going out.
Gently, let your attention widen. Feel the weight of your body on your seat again, your feet on the floor.
What you've just done, over these few minutes, is meditate. Not a failed attempt, not a rough draft. Real meditation.
You sat down, you watched your breath, your mind may have wandered, and you found your way back to the breath.
Everything else in this course builds on these simple steps.
Whenever you're ready, open your eyes, or slowly lift your gaze.
During your day, you can come back to one conscious breath, anywhere at all. Just one is enough to bring you back here.
Thank you for taking this time for yourself. See you tomorrow, for day two.

sessions.title: Day 2 · The wandering mind
script: There you are. It's good to have you back for day two.
Yesterday, you learned to sit and rest your attention on your breath. Today, we'll take a closer look at something that happens to everyone, within the first few seconds: the mind wandering off.
Settle in the way you did yesterday. Feet on the floor, back upright without being stiff, hands resting.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze drop toward the floor.
Take a slightly fuller breath in through your nose, and let it out slowly through your mouth.
One more, letting your jaw loosen as you breathe out.
[pause 3s]
Then let your breathing return to normal.
Today, your anchor is the belly. That's often where the breath is slowest, and easiest to follow.
If you like, rest one hand on your belly, just below your navel.
Feel it rise gently under your palm as the air comes in. And sink back as the air goes out.
You don't need to breathe harder to feel it. Let the movement be as small as it is.
Belly rising. Belly falling.
You might notice the texture of that movement. The fabric stretching slightly under your fingers, the warmth of your hand, your belly rounding out and then softening.
Maybe notice the little pause at the end of the out-breath, before the next in-breath arrives all by itself.
[pause 3s]
Now I'm going to tell you something important. In a few moments, maybe even already, your mind is going to wander off.
You'll find yourself thinking about a message you need to answer, what's for dinner tonight, a conversation from yesterday.
That's not failure. That's what a human mind does. It makes thoughts the way your heart beats, without asking permission.
And these wanderings are actually useful. Without them, there'd be nothing to train.
Because the heart of meditation isn't staying perfectly focused. It's the moment you realize your mind has drifted, and you bring it back.
That move has three steps. Let's learn them together.
Step one: notice. At some point, you realize, "Oh, I was thinking." That little click is already a moment of presence.
Step two: let go. You don't need to finish the thought, or push it away. You just set it down, the way you'd put an object on a table.
Step three: come back. You gently bring your attention back to your belly, to the breath that's happening right now.
Notice, let go, come back. No judging, no sighing at yourself.
The tone really matters. Picture a puppy wandering off down the sidewalk. You don't scold it. You just bring it back, kindly, as many times as it takes.
Okay, let's practice. Stay with the movement of your belly, under your hand.
[pause 3s]
If your mind has wandered, simply come back. Belly rising, belly falling.
There's nothing to prove here. This isn't a concentration test. It's more like training yourself to be kind to your attention.
Maybe there's a thought here right now. No need to work out where it came from, or whether it matters. Let it be, and find the breath again.
[pause 3s]
Sometimes the mind doesn't leave all at once. It drifts. One thought leads to another, and another, and suddenly you're far away, with no idea how you got there.
That's normal too. As soon as you notice, however far you've traveled, the way back is the same: one breath, right here.
Every time you come back, you're doing a rep. Exactly like a curl for a muscle.
Nobody gets strong by lifting a weight once. You get strong by doing it again, and again, and again.
It's the same here. Your attention gets stronger with every return, not just in the moments when everything feels calm.
So a session where your mind wanders a hundred times is a hundred reps. That's not a bad session. That's a full workout.
Find the in-breath again, right there, under your hand. Then the out-breath, a little longer, unrolling on its own.
If it helps, you can silently say "rising" as your belly swells, and "falling" as it softens. Just a small marker, kept very light.
[pause 3s]
If you've just realized you were thinking about something else, enjoy that moment. You've just woken up from the thought. That's exactly the move.
And if a bit of frustration shows up because it keeps happening, you can notice that too. Frustration is just one more thought. Set it down, and come back.
Gently, let your hand return to your thigh, if it was resting on your belly.
One last word before we finish, about keeping count. Don't try to figure out how many times your mind wandered today. Ten times, fifty times, it doesn't matter at all.
What matters is each return. And now you know how to come back.
And if it feels like you spent almost the whole session somewhere else, you still practiced. Every single time you realized it, that was a return.
Notice, let go, come back. You can take those three words with you.
Later today, when you catch yourself spinning in thought at your screen or on your commute, you can make the same move: notice, and come back to one breath.
Now feel the contact of your body with your seat, and the sounds in the room.
Open your eyes whenever you like, and take a moment to look around.
Tomorrow, we'll discover another anchor, one that's especially helpful when your mind is racing: your body.

sessions.title: Day 3 · Coming home to your body
script: Welcome to day three.
For two days now, you've been leaning on your breath. Today, you'll discover a second anchor, broader, and often easier when your mind is spinning: your body.
For this session, you can stay seated the way you have been, or lie on your back, on a bed or a mat.
If you're lying down, let your arms rest by your sides and your legs fall slightly apart. A pillow under your knees can ease your lower back. If you're on a chair, keep your feet flat on the floor.
Close your eyes, if that feels comfortable.
Take two easy breaths, letting each out-breath last a little longer than the in-breath.
[pause 3s]
Why the body? Because your thoughts are always traveling. Back to this morning's meeting, ahead to tomorrow's to-do list.
Your body doesn't travel. It's always here, right now. A sensation can only ever happen in the present.
When stress has your head spinning, coming back to your body is a bit like stepping onto solid ground.
And if following your breath sometimes makes you a little tense, the body offers a simpler, steadier place to rest.

There's nothing special you're supposed to feel today. No required relaxation. We're simply going to visit the body, the way you might walk through a home you've lived in for years without ever really looking at it.
Start with the points of contact, the places where your body touches something.
First, your feet. Feel them against the floor, or the mattress. Maybe the pressure under your heels, the texture of a sock, a sense of warmth or coolness.
Next, where you're sitting or lying. The weight of your hips on the chair, or your back on the bed. Notice how that support holds you up, without you doing a thing.
You can even hand over a little more of your weight to it, as if you could stop holding yourself up.
And your hands, wherever they're resting. The fabric under your fingers, maybe the warmth of your skin, maybe a faint tingling.
[pause 3s]
Now we'll move through the body, as if a beam of attention were slowly traveling from bottom to top. There's nothing to change. You're just noticing what's there.
If there's nothing in particular to feel in one area, that's useful information too. You just move on to the next.
And if any area is painful, you don't have to stay there. Just note it, and keep going.
Come back to your feet. Your toes, one at a time if you can. The soles, the heels, the tops of your feet.
Maybe some toes feel very clear, and others you can't feel at all. That's really common. You simply notice whatever you can perceive.
Move up into your ankles, your calves, your shins. Notice whether your legs feel heavy or light, tight or loose.
Your knees, then your thighs, the whole weight of your thighs.
Notice where the backs of your thighs meet the chair or the mattress. The pressure, the warmth, maybe the fabric of your clothes.
Your pelvis, your hips. A place where we often hold tension without realizing it.

And your back. The lower back, the middle, then the upper back, between your shoulder blades. If you notice stiffness, just notice it. You might imagine your out-breath flowing through that spot, softening it a little.
[pause 3s]
Now come to your belly. Feel it rise and fall with the breath. Maybe it's knotted, maybe it's soft. Both are welcome.
Your chest. Its movement, subtle or big. Maybe even your heartbeat, if you can feel it.
There's no need to change the rhythm. Let your chest do its work, and simply be the one who witnesses it.
Your shoulders. They often carry a good part of the day. Notice how high they're sitting. If they'd like to drop half an inch, let them.
Then your arms, your elbows, forearms, wrists. And back to your hands, all the way to your fingertips. Maybe notice a pulse, a tingling, or simply their weight.
If your mind slipped away somewhere during this journey, that's fine. Just pick up wherever you remember being, or come back to your hands.
Move up to the back of your neck, the part that holds your head up all day. Let it rest on the pillow if you're lying down, or balance easily on your spine if you're sitting.
Notice your throat as well, at the front of your neck. You can swallow once, and feel that small movement.
Your face. Your jaw, where you can leave a little space between your teeth. Your cheeks. The area around your eyes, which can rest. Your forehead, which can widen and smooth out.
Your tongue can rest easily in your mouth, without pressing against the roof.
[pause 3s]
And finally, the top of your head. Maybe a faint sensation, maybe nothing at all. Simply the highest point of your body.
Now widen your attention to take in the whole body at once, from your feet to the top of your head.
As if you switched from a flashlight to daylight. You're no longer looking at one detail. You're feeling the whole.
Feel this whole body breathing. Air coming in, and your whole body opening a little. Air going out, and your whole body settling.
Notice that the breath isn't only in your nose or your chest. It gently moves your belly, your ribs, your back, sometimes even your shoulders.
[pause 3s]
If your mind wandered along the way, you already know what to do. Notice, let go, come back. Here, you just come back to a sensation, any sensation. The weight of your hands, for example.
Maybe notice how you feel now, compared with the beginning. A little more settled, or not. There's nothing to achieve. Just something to notice.
Gently, start to move a little. Your fingers, your toes. Maybe a stretch, if your body asks for one.
Keep this in mind: your body is an anchor you carry everywhere.
In a line at the store, before a meeting, in the middle of a day that's far too full, you can come back to your feet on the floor, or the weight of your hands. A few seconds is enough.
You can even do it with your eyes open, and no one around you will ever know.
When the moment feels right, open your eyes.
Tomorrow, we'll tune in to sounds, and you'll discover how to watch your thoughts go by.

sessions.title: Day 4 · Sounds and thoughts
script: Day four. You now have two anchors: your breath and your body.
Today, we're shifting perspective a little. Instead of choosing one spot and coming back to it, you'll learn to watch whatever passes through. Sounds first. Then thoughts.
Settle into your usual posture. Back upright, shoulders relaxed, hands resting.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest toward the floor.
Take three easy breaths. Breathe in through your nose, and let the air flow out slowly.
[pause 3s]
Once more, feeling your feet on the floor. And one last time, letting your face soften.
[pause 3s]
Now, open up your listening.
There's nothing to search for. Just let sounds come to you, as if your ears had grown a little wider.
Start with the sounds closest to you. Maybe your own breathing. The rustle of your clothes when you move. The hum of a fridge, a computer, a fan.
There are even sounds inside you. A swallow, a little gurgle, a faint ringing in your ears.
Then reach a little further. Sounds from the next room, from the building. A door, footsteps, a voice.
And further still, outside. The street, a passing car, a bird, the wind, maybe a background hush.
You don't need to strain or make any effort. Your hearing does the work on its own. You just stay here, in the middle of the sounds, like the center of a big circle.
[pause 3s]
Try not to put names on what you hear. Not "car," not "neighbor."
Listen to the sound itself instead. Is it high or low? Loud or soft? Steady, or made of little bursts? Does it come from your left, your right, from behind you?
It's a bit like listening to a language you don't speak. You hear the music, without looking for meaning.
Now notice something surprising. Sounds arrive and leave all on their own.
You don't have to go and get them. You don't have to make them go away.
A sound appears, it lasts a while, then it fades. And another one takes its place.
If you can, try to catch the beginning of a sound, then its end. And the silent space between two sounds.
That silence isn't empty. It's a bit like a blank page, where sounds come to write themselves, and then fade away again.
Some sounds are pleasant, others a bit irritating. A siren, a hammer, a conversation that's too loud.
You can listen to those too, with the same curiosity. Maybe notice how your body reacts, a slight bracing, a tightening. And notice that this sound, too, eventually passes.
You may have noticed something else as well. As soon as a sound arrives, your mind tends to tell a story about it.
"That's the upstairs neighbor. He's always noisy at this time. I really should say something."
The sound lasted two seconds. The story can go on much, much longer.
And that story isn't a sound anymore. It's a thought.
Which brings us to the next step. What you've just noticed with sounds is also true of thoughts.
A thought arrives. An image, a memory, a sentence in your head, a list of things to do.
It stays for a while. Then, if you don't hold on to it, it leaves. And another one arrives.
You don't really choose which thoughts show up, any more than you choose the sounds from the street. But you can choose not to follow every one of them.
Thoughts are like a radio playing in another room. You don't need to switch it off. And you don't need to listen to every program either.
You can let them chatter in the background, and stay quietly where you are.
A thought isn't an order. It isn't necessarily the truth, either. It's just something happening in the mind, passing through, the way a sound passes through the air.
To help with this, I'm going to offer you a little tool: mental noting.
When something catches your attention, you note it with a single word, very softly, inside.
If it's a sound, you note "sound." If it's a thought, you note "thinking." If it's something in your body, an itch, some tension, warmth, you note "feeling."
Just one word, placed lightly, like a feather. Not an analysis, not a judgment.
And right after the label, you let the thing carry on its way.
For example: a car goes by, "sound." You wonder whether you locked the door, "thinking." Your knee tingles, "feeling."
You don't need to note everything. Just whatever calls you most strongly, every few seconds, at your own pace.
And if you're not sure which word to use, that's fine. You can just note "this."
Many people find that this small word creates a welcome bit of distance. You're no longer swept along by the thought. You're seeing it.
Let's try it now, together. I'll speak only now and then, just to guide you along.
Rest in your listening, and let whatever comes, come.
[pause 3s]
Sound. Thinking. Feeling. Just one word, and let it pass.
[pause 3s]
If you realize you've followed a thought a long way, you can note "thinking," with a little smile, and come back to listening.
You may notice that some thoughts keep coming back. The same worry, the same list. Each time, it's simply "thinking," without asking yourself why it's back.
Notice how a label creates a bit of space. You're no longer inside the thought. You're watching it go by, like a car in the street.
[pause 3s]
Sometimes nothing in particular shows up. Just a calm background, a faint hum. You can rest there, without noting anything, until something calls you.
And sometimes everything arrives at once. A noise, an itch, three thoughts. Just pick whatever is strongest, note it, and leave the rest in the background.
If you feel drowsy, or a kind of fog rolls in, you can note that too: "tired." Then sit up a little straighter, and come back to listening.
Keep the label light. If it starts to feel like effort, or you catch yourself hunting for the perfect word, drop it and simply listen.
Gently, set the labels aside.
Come back to your breath. Feel the air coming in, and going out. Your belly, your chest, wherever it's clearest.
[pause 3s]
Maybe notice how you are right now. Calmer, more restless, or about the same as when you started. All of it is fine. There was nothing to achieve.
What you practiced today is a different way of being with what goes on inside you: not following everything, not fighting everything. Just watching it pass.
You didn't need to quiet your mind, or the world around you. You simply changed the way you stand in the middle of it all.
Later today, when a thought keeps looping, you can try giving it its label, "thinking," and letting it drift off like the sound of a car in the street.
Feel your body on your seat again. Move your hands a little.
And whenever you feel like it, open your eyes.
Tomorrow, we'll turn toward what's often the trickiest thing to observe: your emotions.

sessions.title: Day 5 · Making room for feelings
script: How are you, right now?
Not the answer you give by the coffee machine, "fine, thanks, you?" The real answer, the one that's there when you stop for a second.
That's the question for day five. Today, we'll learn to make room for what you feel.
Settle into your usual posture. Plant your feet, gently lengthen your back, let your hands rest.
Close your eyes, or keep a low, soft gaze.
Take a few breaths at your own pace. Feel the air coming in, and going out.
[pause 3s]
Rest your attention on your breath, wherever it's clearest for you. Your nostrils, your chest, or your belly.
You know this place by now. It's your starting point, and your safe harbor whenever you need it.
Stay with it for a few breaths. If your mind wanders, bring it back, the way you know how.
[pause 3s]
Now, without changing anything, ask yourself: what's my mood, right at this moment?
You don't need to find a big emotion. Maybe some tiredness. A bit of impatience. A slight worry. Calm. Or a fuzzy mix that's hard to put into words.
If it feels blurry, you can ask yourself what the weather is like inside you. Bright sunshine, a hazy sky, fog, light drizzle, a stiff wind? Often an image comes more easily than a word.
Everything is welcome. Even "I don't know" is an honest answer.
The idea isn't to change what's here. Just to acknowledge it, the way you'd nod hello to someone walking into the room.
For this first time, it's best to stay with an everyday emotion, not the hardest thing in your life.
And if whatever shows up feels very heavy today, you can choose to stay with your breath, or your feet on the floor. That's a perfectly good choice.
An emotion isn't just an idea in your head. You can feel it in your body too.
Stress often tightens the jaw or the shoulders. Worry can knot the stomach. Sadness sometimes weighs on the chest, or tightens the throat. Joy can feel like warmth spreading outward.
These are just examples. For you, it may be different.
So explore gently. Where does this mood live in you, right now?
Check your throat. Your chest. Your belly. Check your shoulders too, your jaw, your hands.
[pause 3s]
If you find something, look at it with curiosity, as if you were discovering it for the very first time.
Is it warm or cool? Tight or spread out? Heavy or buzzing? Does it have a shape, a size, edges?
Is it still, or does it move a little, pulse, spread?
You don't need to describe it perfectly. A few rough words are enough.
Sometimes the feeling is tiny, just a slight tightness or a faint heaviness. Small is enough. You don't need anything dramatic to practice with.
And if you can't feel anything specific, that's perfectly fine too. You can simply stay with the overall feeling of your body, right now.
You can also check some quieter places: the pit of your stomach, the back of your throat, your forehead. Sometimes an emotion hides there as a small knot of tension.
Now, name what's here, simply, in everyday words.
One small shift makes a big difference. Instead of saying "I'm irritated," try "there's some irritation here." Or "there's tiredness." "There's sadness."
Can you feel the difference? The emotion is here, but it isn't all of you. It's something you're feeling, not who you are.
Many people notice that just finding the right word for what they feel makes things a little clearer, and a little less overwhelming.
Say that word silently, once, in a gentle tone.
[pause 3s]
And now, breathe around this sensation.
Imagine your in-breath surrounding it, without pushing on it, like air flowing around an object resting on a table.
And with each out-breath, a little more space opening up around it. As if the room it's in were growing larger.
You're not trying to make it go away. You're making room for it. As if you were saying, "You can be here."
[pause 3s]
If you notice yourself bracing against it, something inside saying "no, not this," you can notice that resistance too. It's human. And you can soften it, just a tiny bit, on the out-breath.
Breathe in, feeling the air surround the sensation. Breathe out, letting your belly and shoulders loosen around it, just a little.
Often, when we stop fighting an emotion, it shifts a little. It loosens, it moves, or it softens.
Sometimes it stays exactly as it is. And that's fine too. Your only job is to give it space.

For a few breaths, watch it the way you'd watch the sea from the beach. A wave rises, peaks, then falls back. Is the intensity exactly the same from one breath to the next? Or does it change a little?
If at any point it's too much, you can always come back to your feet on the floor, or open your eyes. You're always in charge.
There's no right answer to find here. You're simply learning to keep yourself company, with patience.
If you'd like, place a hand on your heart. Or on your belly, or wherever you feel the emotion.
Feel the warmth of your palm, its light weight, the movement of your breath beneath it.
If this gesture feels odd or a bit awkward, that's normal the first time. You can also simply rest one hand on top of the other, in your lap.
It's a simple gesture your body understands well. A bit like a friend's hand on your shoulder.
And now, offer yourself a kind sentence, silently. For example: "This is hard right now, and that's human." Or simply: "I'm here for myself."
You can choose your own words. The ones you'd say to someone you love, if they were feeling the same thing.
[pause 3s]
Stay a moment longer with your hand resting there, and your breath coming and going.
[pause 3s]
Gently, you can let your hand come down. Come back to your breath, wherever it's clearest.
Then to your whole body, held by your seat.
Notice how you feel now, compared with when you started, without needing anything to have changed.
Keep this in mind: feeling something is not a failure of meditation. Meditating doesn't mean always being calm. It means being present with what's here, even when it's uncomfortable.
An emotion is something you feel in the body. And, like yesterday's sounds, it eventually passes.
Even a few seconds spent noticing an emotion, instead of being swept away by it, is real practice.
Later today, when an emotion rises, you can come back to these three steps: feel it in the body, name it, make a little room for it.
And if a heavy emotion keeps coming back and weighs on your daily life, talking to a health professional can really help.
When the moment feels right, open your eyes, and take your time coming back.
Tomorrow, we'll bring together everything you've learned, and get a taste of something more spacious.

sessions.title: Day 6 · Simply being here
script: Welcome to day six.
So far, you've learned to place your attention somewhere: on the breath, on the body, on sounds. You've also learned to watch thoughts and emotions pass by.
Today, you're going to let go of the anchor, just for a little while. Not to get lost, but to discover what it's like to simply be here, welcoming whatever shows up.
In meditation traditions, this is sometimes called open awareness. You'll see, it's much simpler than it sounds.
We'll take it step by step. First the breath, then the body, then sounds and thoughts. At each step, we open a little wider, without letting go of what was already there.
Take your time to settle in. Feel your seat, your back lengthening without effort, your shoulders settling down.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest ahead of you, toward the floor, not focusing on anything.
And give yourself a big breath, like the sigh you let out when you get home after a long day.
[pause 3s]
One more, letting your upper body soften as you breathe out.
[pause 3s]
Begin with your most familiar anchor: the breath.
Find it wherever it's clearest. Follow one in-breath from beginning to end. Then one out-breath, from beginning to end.
Notice that each breath is a little different from the last. Shorter, longer, deeper.
[pause 3s]
Let your breath bring you back here, one breath after another. No need to control it. Just watch it do its thing.
If your mind is already wandering, you know the way back.
Now gently widen your attention to include the whole body.
As if a flashlight beam were opening up until it lit the entire room.
You feel the breath, and around it, the whole body. The weight on your seat. Your feet. Your hands. The temperature of the air on your skin.
You don't need to move from one area to the next, like in the body scan. You're feeling the whole body at once, a little blurry, like a landscape seen from a distance.
A landscape with calm areas and livelier ones, warm spots and cool spots.
[pause 3s]
If a stronger sensation catches your attention, an itch, some tension in your back, let it be there, in the landscape, without locking onto it.
It's part of the picture. It isn't the whole picture.
Notice too that this landscape is always changing. One area warms up, another fades, the breath gently shifts the sensations around. Nothing stays fixed.
And now, add sounds.
The body breathing, and around it, the sounds of the room, the street, the world. All of it can live side by side in your attention.
There's nothing to choose. The body is here. The sounds are here. They come and go.
Notice that you don't need to reach out for sounds. They come to you, all on their own, just as the body makes itself felt on its own.

The body and the sounds aren't two things to monitor one after the other. They're here together, in the same space. Like sitting at a café terrace: you feel the sun on your skin, and at the same time you hear the street, without any effort.
[pause 3s]
And then, thoughts. They're part of the landscape too. A thought appears, like a sound. It stays for a while, then drifts away.
You don't need to follow it, or stop it. You can let it pass, the way you let the sound of a car pass.
If you like, you can still use the labels from day four: "thinking," "sound," "feeling." Or simply let everything pass, without words.
You may notice that some thoughts are light and pass quickly. Others are sticky, they come back, they insist. Those can stay in the background too, without you having to obey them.
Emotions, if there are any, have their place as well. You now know how to welcome them in the body, give them a name, and make a little room for them.
An image might help here. Picture the sky.
Clouds drift across it, small or large, light or dark. Birds, planes, sometimes a storm.
The sky doesn't choose what passes through it. It doesn't hold on to anything. It doesn't push anything away.
And even in the biggest storm, the sky is still the sky. Vast, open, untouched behind the clouds.
If you've ever flown on a rainy day, you know this: above the gray layer, the blue was there all along.
Your awareness can be like that sky. Thoughts, sounds, sensations, emotions are the clouds. They pass. The sky remains.
You don't have to become the sky through effort. You just have to stop chasing every cloud.

And notice something, very gently. Something in you is watching all of this go by. The sounds, the thoughts, the sensations. That quiet awareness doesn't leave with them. It's simply here, like the sky.
[pause 3s]
For the next few minutes, I'll say very little. Simply rest in this openness, like the sky. Let everything come, let everything go.
There's nothing to do. Nothing to get right. Just be here.
[pause 3s]
Let your attention rest, without holding on to anything. Like an open hand, rather than a clenched fist.
Breath, body, sounds, thoughts. Everything passes through the sky of your awareness.
You can feel the breath coming and going, in the middle of everything else. It's no longer at the center. It's part of the landscape too.
Maybe a distant sound appears, then fades. You let it pass through, without following it to the end.
A memory, a plan for tonight, a small worry. Just another cloud. It comes, it goes.
[pause 3s]
Maybe a sensation shows up in the body. Some warmth, a tingling, a spot of tension. You let it appear, linger, and change.
Notice that you don't need to decide where to look. Whatever is here shows up, and whatever leaves, leaves.
If you notice that a thought has taken over, that's normal. A cloud doesn't damage the sky.
You can come back to the breath first, for a few breaths, to steady yourself. Then, without hurrying, open your attention back up to everything else.
Maybe notice the quality of this moment. A bit of space. A bit of calm. Or restlessness instead. The sky welcomes it all.
If you catch yourself waiting for something, a special kind of calm, a feeling of spaciousness, notice that waiting too. It's just another cloud.
Sounds nearby, sounds far away. The silence between them. All of it held together, effortlessly.
Between two thoughts, there's sometimes a little gap. A moment where nothing in particular is happening. You can enjoy it, without trying to stretch it out.
[pause 3s]
Your body breathes on its own. Sounds arrive on their own. Thoughts pass on their own. And all you have to do is be here.
Nothing to hold on to. Nothing to push away. Just this moment, and then the next.
If you notice yourself straining to keep your attention open, ease off the effort. Openness comes more easily when you stop chasing it.
There's no special experience to reach. Just the one that's here, now.
If the openness starts to feel too vague, or your mind gets restless, return to the breath for as long as you need. The anchor is always there. And when you feel steadier, you can open up again.
Gently, bring your attention back to the breath. One breath in, one breath out.
Then feel your body again, resting here. The weight of your hands, the contact of your feet.
Take a moment to notice how you feel, without demanding anything. Maybe a little lighter, maybe tired, maybe exactly the same. All of it is fine.
If this openness felt pleasant, wonderful. If it felt strange or hard to grasp, that's very common at first. It's a quality you discover little by little, often in small glimpses.
As with everything else this week, it isn't a question of talent. It's a question of getting familiar with it.
Today, you used everything you've learned this week.
The breath to anchor you. Coming back, when your mind wanders. The body as a place to rest. Sounds and labels to watch things pass. Making room for what you feel.
And you got a taste, maybe just for a few seconds, of that wider space that's always there, behind the busyness.
Those few seconds count. With practice, they become easier to find again.
You can find them outside meditation, too. On a park bench, on a moving train, looking out a window. A few moments when you let everything in, without sorting any of it.
During your day, if you think of it, look up at the sky, the real one. And remember that your thoughts pass, and you remain.
Whenever you're ready, move a little, stretch if you feel like it, and open your eyes.
Tomorrow, on the last day of this course, we'll look at how to take meditation with you.

sessions.title: Day 7 · Take it with you
script: Day seven. You've reached the end of this course.
Take a second to notice that. Seven times this week, you chose to stop for a few minutes. No need to make a big deal of it, but it's worth acknowledging.
And if you skipped a day or two along the way, that's fine too. You picked it back up, and that's exactly the skill you've been learning.
Today, we'll do two things. A short, complete practice that brings together everything you've learned. Then some time to plan what comes next, in concrete terms.
Settle in the way you're now used to. Feet down, back upright, hands at rest.
Close your eyes, or gently lower your gaze.
Let's start with the breath.
Take two slightly deeper breaths, to arrive. Breathe in through your nose, and let the air flow out, long and slow.
[pause 3s]
Then let your breath return to its own rhythm. Find the place where it's clearest, and rest your attention there.
The coolness of air at your nostrils, your chest rising, or your belly swelling. You know by now where it is for you.
[pause 3s]
If your mind wanders, you know the move. Notice, let go, come back.
[pause 3s]
Now widen your attention to your body. The points of contact first: your feet on the floor, the weight of your hips, your hands.
Feel how the floor and the seat hold you up, without you having to make the slightest effort.
Then, in a single sweep, the whole body. From your feet to your head. Notice the tense areas, the relaxed areas, without fixing anything.
If your shoulders or your jaw want to let go, let them.
[pause 3s]

Do a quick check-in with what you're feeling, like on day five. What's your mood, right now? Where does it live in your body? Name it simply, "there's tiredness," "there's joy," and let it have its place.
And finally, open up to everything else. The sounds around you, near and far. The thoughts passing by. Emotions, if there are any.
Like yesterday's sky, you let everything move through, without holding on, without pushing away.
Sounds arriving, thoughts passing, sensations shifting. You stay here, open, and watch life unfold.
[pause 3s]
A thought, a sound, a sensation. Everything comes, everything goes. If you get lost, the breath is waiting, and then you open up again.
Gently come back to the breath, simply, for a few breaths.
[pause 3s]
What you've just done in a few minutes sums up the whole week. Three key skills, easy to remember.
Anchor: rest your attention on something steady, the breath or the body.
Notice: realize that your mind has wandered, or that an emotion is here, without judging yourself.
Come back: bring your attention back, kindly, as many times as it takes.
Anchor, notice, come back. Everything else grows from that.
You've already practiced all three this week, sometimes without even realizing it. They're yours now.
You can do these three things in three minutes on your cushion, or in three seconds in a checkout line. It's the same skill, at different scales.
Keep your eyes closed, or your gaze low. We're going to plan what comes next, in this same calm state.
Because a meditation practice that lasts isn't a matter of willpower. It's a matter of habit.
Willpower is like a battery. It's full on Monday morning, and often drained by Thursday night. A habit keeps working even when the battery is flat.
And a habit sticks best when it has a set time and a trigger.
It's like a path across a field: the more often you walk it, the easier it is to find.
When the time and place are decided in advance, you don't have to negotiate with yourself every single day. The decision has already been made.
The trigger is something you already do every day, without thinking about it. Your new habit attaches right after it, like a carriage hooked onto a train that's already moving.
For example: after my first coffee. Before I open my email. When I get home from work, before I sit down on the couch. Right after I brush my teeth at night.
To help you choose, run through an ordinary day in your mind, from waking up to going to bed. Where's a small gap, a moment that comes back every day, at roughly the same time?
Take a moment to choose yours. A realistic moment, one that really exists in your days, even the busiest ones.
[pause 3s]
Got it? If nothing comes to mind, that's okay. You can come back to it after this session.
If you have one, put it into a simple sentence, silently. "After my coffee, I sit for three minutes." A clear sentence is much easier to follow than a vague intention.
Think too about what might trip you up. Oversleeping, a sick child, a meeting that runs late.
And plan your backup right now. For example: if I miss my morning moment, I'll take three conscious breaths before bed. That way, the chain doesn't break.
As for length, keep it modest. Three minutes every day beats twenty minutes once in a while. You can always do more, on the days you feel like it.
You can also set the stage. Leave your cushion where you can see it, or keep your phone within reach at that time, with the app already open.
Now, imagine tomorrow. Picture that moment as precisely as you can.
Where are you? In your kitchen, your living room, your office? What's the light like? What sounds can you hear?
See yourself finishing your trigger. Setting down your mug, closing the door, putting away your toothbrush.
Then see yourself sitting down, closing your eyes, and staying there for three minutes, with your breath.
Maybe you can already feel your feet on the floor, in that place. The air coming in, the air going out.
See your mind wander, once or twice, toward the day ahead. And see yourself coming back, without any self-blame. That's all part of it.
Then see the end of those three minutes. You open your eyes, and carry on with your day, with a little more space.
Notice what it feels like, to see yourself taking this time for you.
Maybe a little pride, a little calm. Or a bit of resistance, a voice saying "I won't have time." You can welcome that too, and keep your intention.
[pause 3s]
And if tomorrow doesn't go to plan, that's not failure. You simply start again the next day. It's the same move once more: notice, and come back.
Outside of these set moments, meditation can slip into your day anywhere, in tiny doses.
Three conscious breaths at a red light, or while you wait for the train.
Feeling your feet on the floor while the coffee machine runs.
Listening to the sounds of the street for thirty seconds, like on day four, letting the noises come and go.
Noticing a thought and labeling it, "thinking," during a tense meeting.
Placing a hand on your heart before a difficult call.
Letting your shoulders and jaw relax every time you open a door, or your phone buzzes.
Or, before you eat, taking one breath and really looking at your plate for a few seconds.
Pick just one to start with. The one that speaks to you most.
These micro-practices don't replace a sitting session, but they weave a thread of presence through your whole day. And little by little, that thread makes your sessions easier too.
[pause 3s]
Now come back to your breath, and to your whole body, here.
This course is ending, but your practice is really just beginning.
Remember that consistency matters more than perfection. One missed day doesn't erase anything you've built.
You can repeat these seven days whenever you like. Many people discover new things the second time around, because they're not quite the same person anymore.
In CortiFree, you'll find other paths, depending on what you need.
If your nights are difficult, explore the Sleep theme. If your days put you under pressure, try the At work sessions, or Stress SOS for the moments when it all overflows.
If emotions take up a lot of space, the Anxiety and emotions theme builds on what you discovered on day five. And if you'd like to be gentler with yourself, the Kindness theme is made for that.
To go deeper, Body and relaxation offers longer body scans, and Focus and clarity trains your attention even further.
You don't need to explore everything. Simply choose whatever fits your life right now.
And if one day meditation seems to stop working, the session "When it doesn't seem to work" is there for you.
When the moment feels right, tune back in to the sounds around you, gently move your hands, and open your eyes.
Thank you for walking this path. See you tomorrow, at your moment.

sessions.title: When it doesn't seem to work
script: If you're listening to this session, maybe meditation isn't going the way you imagined.
You get restless, you nod off, or a little voice tells you it's pointless.
Here's the good news: if you're here, you haven't given up. And these three obstacles are so common that meditation traditions have been describing them for centuries.
They don't mean you're doing it wrong. They mean you're practicing.
We'll look at them one at a time, and for each one, you'll try a small adjustment, right now.
Get as comfortable as you can. For now, keep your eyes open, your gaze resting on the floor.
[pause 3s]
First obstacle: restlessness. A fidgety body, a racing mind, the feeling that you just can't sit still.
Instead of fighting it, try three things.
First, keep your eyes open. When closing them lets your mind run wild, a gaze resting on the floor often helps you steady.
Next, give your mind something to do: count your breaths.
And finally, lengthen your out-breath a little. An out-breath that's longer than the in-breath can help your body slow down.
Let's try it. Breathe in normally through your nose. Then, on the out-breath, silently count "one," letting the air flow out slowly.
Breathe in. And on the out-breath, "two."
[pause 3s]
Three… the air flows out slowly, without forcing.
Four… your shoulders can drop.
Five… and back to one.
Carry on at your own pace, silently. One out-breath, one number, up to five. If you lose count, just go back to one, no big deal.
[pause 3s]
If you feel a little light-headed, simply let your breathing return to normal.
Notice how counting keeps your mind just busy enough to stay put. The point isn't to reach five. The point is to notice when you've lost the thread, and start again.
Notice, too, what happens in your body as the out-breath lengthens. Maybe your shoulders drop a little, your belly softens. Or maybe nothing obvious, and that's fine as well.
And if your body really needs to move, listen to it. A short walk, a stretch before you sit down, and the session often gets easier.
Second obstacle: sleepiness. You close your eyes, and ten seconds later, your head is nodding.
First of all, this is often an honest signal: you may simply need more rest. It's not a fault. It's information.
But if you'd like to stay clear-headed, here's what helps.
Straighten your back. Imagine the top of your head rising a little toward the ceiling. Sit away from the backrest, if you can.
Open your eyes, and let some light in.
And take a slightly fuller breath in through your nose, feeling the cool air at the edge of your nostrils.
Try it now. Back straight, eyes open, one fresh breath in.
[pause 3s]
Notice the difference, even if it's small. A little more light, a little more presence in your back and in your eyes.
Going forward, you can also meditate by an open window, standing up, or at a time of day when you're less tired. Right after a big meal, for example, tends to be harder.
Third obstacle, the sneakiest one: doubt. "This is pointless." "I'm terrible at meditating." "This just isn't for me."
These sentences sound like facts. But look at them closely: they're thoughts. Just like "I need to buy bread."
You don't have to believe them, or fight them. You can note them, like any other thought.
You can even get curious: when do they tend to show up? Often, right when a session gets a little boring or uncomfortable.
And the effects of practice are often subtle. They show up less during the session than during your day: noticing a little sooner that you're tense, taking a breath before you reply.
Let's try. Come back to the breath, at your belly or your nostrils.
And as soon as a doubting thought appears, something like "am I doing this right?", simply note "doubt," lightly. Then come back to the breath.
[pause 3s]
Doubt. And back to the breath.
Other thoughts may show up too: "I'm bored," "when does this end?" They're close cousins of doubt. Same move: a light label, and back to the breath.
If no doubting thoughts show up, great. Just notice whatever is here.
Doubt often comes from comparing yourself with some ideal meditation, calm and glowing, that only exists in advertisements. Your real meditation is today's, with whatever it holds.
And if your session feels like a mountain, make it shorter. Three minutes done beats ten minutes dreaded.
You could also keep a small notebook: one line a day, noting how you feel after your session. After a few weeks, the subtle changes become much easier to see.
Before we finish, I want to tell you something important.
A meditation that feels like a failure, full of restlessness, sleepiness, or doubt, is often the one that trains you the most.
Because every time you notice and come back, you're doing exactly the move that matters. Calm sessions are pleasant. Difficult sessions are the ones that build you.
So next time it "doesn't work," remember: eyes open and counted breaths for restlessness, a straight back and fresh air for sleepiness, and the label "doubt" for that little voice.
And above all, come back tomorrow. That's the only rule.
